point: The chapter surveys EV flexibility, demand response and modelling approaches to set the thesis scope and spot gaps.
Parts of the chapter were reused from the authors' earlier project thesis and revised.
This section looks at how EVs affect the grid and how literature obtains flexibility from them.
Growing EV numbers in Norway already strain local grids and will add substantial load by 2030.
Higher EV density tends to raise local grid costs, though less so where customer density is high.
EV chargers raise consumption and congestion, forcing costly low-voltage upgrades, although faster smart chargers can ease peak loads.
Large-scale EV integration causes a range of technical grid problems and lowers supply quality.
Uncontrolled EV charging raises peak demand and violates grid limits, so more flexible charging is needed.
Flexibility services from loads such as EVs offer DSOs an alternative to grid reinforcement.
Battery storage is less viable in Norway because of hydropower, but its potential is growing.
Smart charging using historical data and scheduling cuts peaks and relieves transformers compared with greedy charging.
End-user adoption of smart charging depends on safety, technology interest, economic benefits and flexibility.
V2G could supply flexibility to an EV parking lot, and the review focuses on the consumer domain.
A two-stage day-ahead and real-time optimisation of V2G at an office works but struggles with monthly peak demand.
V2G may accelerate battery degradation, so accurate degradation models and compensation to owners are needed.
The section examines how price-based and incentive-based demand response programmes are implemented.
The demand charge is a peak-based tariff component, examined together with long-term effects of short-term decisions.
Including demand charges and storage in optimisation lowers cost, and ignoring the demand charge raises cost substantially.
A metaheuristic weighting short-term price against long-term demand charge cut household costs considerably.
The section shows how earlier studies used incentive-based programmes to give DSOs flexibility and set incentives.
Residential communities can give DSOs voltage support and loss reduction at modest compensation.
Incentive-based programmes combined with flexible resources such as EVs reduce peaks and stabilise the grid.
Longer notice time gives more demand flexibility but larger wind forecast errors, and shorter notice does the opposite.
